content: Early-onset infections in neonates can lead to severe illness or even death during the neonatal period. Prompt administration of antibiotics has been demonstrated to reduce mortality in such cases. However, it remains unclear which specific antibiotic regimen is most appropriate for treating presumed early neonatal sepsis. This review has been replaced by a more recent Cochrane Review conducted by Korang in 2021. The objective of this review was to evaluate and compare the effectiveness and adverse effects of different antibiotic regimens used for the treatment of presumed early neonatal sepsis. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted in several databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, The Cochrane Library, Issue 2, 2003), MEDLINE (from 1966 to August 2003), EMBASE (from 1980 to September 2003), and ZETOC (from 1993 to August 2003). Additionally, pharmaceutical companies were contacted to obtain any unpublished data. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared different antibiotic regimens, including both monotherapies and combination therapies, for the treatment of early neonatal sepsis. Two reviewers independently screened abstracts and full-text reports to determine eligibility based on the inclusion criteria. They also assessed the quality of the studies and extracted relevant data. For dichotomous outcomes, the treatment effect was expressed as relative risk with a 95% confidence interval. A meta-analysis was performed using a fixed-effect model. The main findings of the review were based on two small studies that compared monotherapy with combination therapy. These studies did not demonstrate any significant differences in mortality, treatment failure, or bacteriological resistance between the two approaches. The authors concluded that there is no evidence from randomized trials to suggest that any specific antibiotic regimen is superior to others for the treatment of presumed early neonatal sepsis. Further research is necessary to address this unresolved issue.
